claims.claim: User experience (UX) is the overall experience a person has with a product. The working definition used in this lesson is attributed to Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen of Nielsen Norman Group: user experience encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services, and its products.

The total user experience must be distinguished from the user interface (UI), even though the UI is an extremely important part of the design. Nielsen Norman Group states this distinction explicitly and illustrates it with a movie-review website: even if the UI for finding a film is perfect, the UX is poor for a user who wants information about a small independent release if the underlying database only contains movies from the major studios.

User interface (UI) design is the process designers use to build interfaces in software or computerized devices, focusing on looks or style, with the aim of creating interfaces that users find easy to use and pleasurable (Interaction Design Foundation working definition).

Interfaces come in more than one form: graphical user interfaces (GUIs) such as a computer desktop, voice-controlled interfaces such as smart assistants, and gesture-based interfaces such as those in virtual reality (Interaction Design Foundation).

UX design is broader than UI design: UX design involves the entire process of acquiring and integrating the product, including aspects of branding, design, usability, and function, and the experience includes related touchpoints such as the marketing campaign, packaging, and after-sales support (Interaction Design Foundation).

While usability and user interface (UI) design are important aspects of UX design, they are subsets of it: a UX designer is concerned with the entire process of acquiring and integrating a product (Interaction Design Foundation).
UX and UI are separate disciplines that overlap: job titles such as 'UX/UI designer' exist, but the overlap does not make the two interchangeable (Interaction Design Foundation).

Usability is one part of the larger user experience (UX) umbrella: UX encompasses designing the overall experience of a product, while usability focuses on the mechanics of making sure products work as well as possible for the user (U.S. Digital.gov).

conflictingEvidence.issue: The boundary between UX and UI is described differently across sources: Nielsen Norman Group draws a firm conceptual line (distinguish the total user experience from the UI), while the Interaction Design Foundation emphasizes that the disciplines overlap in practice, as shown by combined job titles like 'UX/UI designer.'
positions: Nielsen Norman Group: the total user experience must be distinguished from the user interface, even though the UI is an extremely important part of the design.
Interaction Design Foundation: while there is overlap between UX and UI, they are separate disciplines; combined job titles are common.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Not a substantive conflict: both sources agree UI is an important part of the broader UX. The lesson presents the conceptual distinction as the core teaching point and the practical overlap (small teams doing both, combined job titles) as the honest framing, attributing each position to its source.

sourceRecords.title: The Definition of User Experience (UX)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Article by Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen, dated August 8, 1998. Supports: the attributed working definition of UX ('user experience encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services, and its products'); the explicit instruction to distinguish total user experience from the user interface (UI) while noting the UI is an extremely important part of the design; and the movie-review-database example showing that a perfect UI cannot compensate for a UX that fails the user's needs. Used for verification and synthesis only; no prose reproduced.
